title: The Great Famine
objective: After this level you can describe the famine that began in 1315 and its causes.
summary: From 1315, torrential rain ruined harvests across northern Europe. Animal disease, soaring prices and war turned bad weather into the worst European famine by share of population.

cards.headline: In 1315 it started raining. For the harvest, it never really stopped.
cards.body: Nobody in northern Europe had seen a summer like it. Then came another. How does rain turn into the worst famine in European history?

cards.headline: The summer that drowned the fields
cards.body: Torrential rain struck France from April 1315 and England from May, and the harvests failed. We don’t only have chroniclers’ word for it. Tree rings, nature’s weather diary, show that the growing seasons of 1314 to 1316 were the fifth wettest in Europe between 1300 and 2012. Picture your garden after a soggy week. Now picture three summers of it.

cards.fact: In England, wheat cost up to eight times as much in 1315 as in 1313.
cards.context: Wheat that sold for five shillings in 1313 fetched as much as forty by 1315. The hunger stretched from Ireland to Poland and from Scandinavia to central France. Measured by deaths as a share of the population, it was the worst famine Europe has known.

cards.headline: Not just the weather
cards.body: Rain started it, but the historian William Chester Jordan shows how much else piled on: diseases that killed farm animals, one failed harvest after another, wild swings in prices, and wars that got in the way of moving food. Full recovery took until 1322. A famine is rarely just about the sky. It is about everything that decides whether food reaches your table.

mascot.line: Keep this: a famine is about more than the weather.

cards.headline: The Great Famine: understood
learned: Northern Europe went hungry from Ireland to Poland
Animal disease, prices and war made it worse
It was Europe’s worst famine by share of deaths

questions.prompt: What set off the Great Famine that began in 1315?

options.label: A long drought that dried up rivers
options.rationale: It was the opposite: far too much water.

options.label: Torrential rain that ruined the harvests
A plague of locusts from Africa
options.rationale: Rain, not insects, ruined the crops.

options.label: An enemy army burning the fields
options.rationale: War made it worse, but rain started it.

questions.explanation: Torrential rain from spring 1315 struck France and England, and the harvests failed.

questions.prompt: According to William Chester Jordan, why was the Great Famine so severe?

options.label: Farmers refused to plant new crops
options.rationale: They planted; the harvests kept failing.

options.label: Kings banned the sale of grain
options.rationale: Prices swung wildly; there was no simple ban.

options.label: Europe had no farms north of the Alps
options.rationale: Northern Europe was farmed; that’s why it hurt.

options.label: Animal disease, failed harvests, price swings and war piled on

questions.explanation: Rain started it, but diseases of farm animals, repeated harvest failures, volatile prices and war made it far worse.

questions.prompt: The Great Famine began in 1315. Which of Level 1’s three periods of the Middle Ages was it part of?

options.label: The high Middle Ages
options.rationale: Those ran from about 1000 to about 1300.

options.label: After the Middle Ages
options.rationale: The Middle Ages lasted until about 1500.

questions.explanation: Level 1 dated the late Middle Ages from about 1300, so 1315 falls near its start.
